Fixed in v2.11.0. g_bShoppedThisBreak was cleared on mvm_wave_begin, which ends a break rather than starts one, so every bot that survived a wave carried 'has shopped' through the next break and GetDesiredBotAction had nothing left to offer an engineer or a medic between rounds. A bot that died shopped normally because a spawn clears the same flag, which is why it looked intermittent and why a vote restart froze the whole team. Cleared when the break opens now, on both mvm_wave_complete and mvm_wave_failed. Measured on Decoy, AUTO_BOTS, two waves cleared either way: share of between-wave samples with no behaviour, engineers 86% and 100% before, 0% and 0% after; medic 100% to 76%, and the medic's own share closed separately. The between-waves table in the run report is the instrument.

Turned from a warning into a check: run.sh reads MemAvailable and refuses to start below 1500 MB, TESTBED_MIN_FREE_MB=0 to override. The reason is in docs/testbed-metrics.md. Verified by forcing the threshold high and watching it stop. Today's 41 runs and 231 waves ran with about 4 GB available and no crash, which is the other half of the same claim.

Fixed. Not a blueprint and not a lost owner: TF2 takes a building out of the player's object list the moment he picks it up, so GetObjectOfType answered none while the engineer was carrying one. The dispenser gate then said 'no dispenser, build one', he placed a fresh one, and when the carried one went down there were two with one engineer. HasObjectOfType counts the carried one and both gates ask it. A kicked bot was ruled out by test: kicking an engineer holding a level three dispenser removed it and left no orphan. Six waves of Coal Town with relocation on: five cleared, no crash, never more than one dispenser at once, sentry uptime 72 per cent.

Fixed and measured. A Rescue Ranger bolt repairs a building and does not reload one; only a wrench hit puts shells back. A sentry at full health with an empty magazine still answers yes to SentryNeedsMetal, so CanRepairFromRange let the engineer stand across the map firing bolts into something already whole, forever. From his point of view he was fixing it, which is why it reads as refusing.

Range repair is for damage only now. The building samples carry the magazine, which nothing counted before.

Coal Town, six waves each way with the Rescue Ranger loadout: samples of a full health sentry under fifty shells 21 of 126 before and 6 of 116 after, median magazine 104 to a full 200, five of six waves cleared either way. Measured rather than assumed, and it is mostly already what he asks for. Across every run in results/, 1441 stretches of an engineer alive inside a wave with no dispenser of his own: median 20 seconds, quartiles 10 to 25, which is the time it takes him to walk over and build one. So he does prioritise it.

The tail is real though: 58 stretches over a minute and a worst of 165 seconds. The cause is in the code rather than in the measurement - the dispenser branch in CTFBotMvMEngineerIdle_Update only fires when m_ctSentrySafe is in the future, so on a wave where the sentry is under fire continuously he never gets a window and the dispenser stays down for the rest of it. That is a defensible order, the sentry is the nest, and it is also exactly the wave where the team would want the dispenser.

Closing as measured. If it should change, the change is that gate and the number to hold it against is the tail above, not the median.

Fixed and measured, and both halves of the report were the same cause.

The sighting rule in Event_PlayerDeath was 'a Spy killed somebody on another team', which a defending Spy satisfies every time he stabs a robot. So the player's own Spy put his whole team on alert, which is why this only happens when somebody plays Spy. A sighting is now a robot's Spy.

The suspect finder also skipped no humans, so a player could be picked as the disguised one. Every robot in this mode is a fake client, so a real player on RED cannot be an enemy Spy. The price is a human on BLU via the mod's join-blue command being unstabbable, which is smaller than a Spy player being frisked by his own team.

Measured with a friendly Spy in the lineup: 187 of 3443 samples spy checking before, 0 of 1676 after. Two lineups without a Spy spent 0 of 8273 samples spy checking, so the trigger was never an actual robot Spy. Firing with a teammate in the crosshair is unchanged at 15 to 18 per cent, which is bots shooting past one another rather than at them, and harmless with friendly fire off.

YES. A pure SourcePawn function compiles and runs under spshell with no game server, no sourcemod.inc and no natives, and its float32 result matches the Go bit for bit.

spshell is not on this machine and not in the SourceMod drop: build.sh pulls the SourceMod tarball, which has no VM shell. Built from alliedmodders/sourcepawn HEAD f2d11ff with AMBuild, about a minute. One patch needed: AMBuildScript sets -Werror and compiler/errors.cpp:241 has a signed/unsigned comparison GCC rejects, since the tree is clang-only.

The test is table driven over 8 inputs including clamp boundaries, an overheal, a value with no exact float32 and a negative distance. Plain float32 equality, no epsilon, all pass. The score crosses the boundary as raw bits, view_as<int> on one side and math.Float32frombits on the other, because printfloat gives six decimals and would hide the drift the test exists to catch. The test was proved able to fail: perturbing the Go side alone to hurt*30.5 reports 77.5 under spshell against 77.79167 in Go.

The fallback named in this bead, a test plugin printing a verdict at server startup, is not needed.

One real finding, filed as spg follow-ups: the SourceMod 1.12 spcomp64 cannot compile for spshell. It implicitly includes its own float.inc declaring the float operators as __FLOAT_DIV__, while spshell binds them lowercase as __float_div, so an SM-compiled plugin dies on the first division with Native is not bound. The differential test compiles with the 1.13 spcomp built beside spshell; the plugin build keeps the SourceMod one.

The feature table is one Go slice and Name is the whole identity: Enum() returns FEATURE_ plus the uppercased name, ConVar() returns sm_redbots_feature_ plus the name. The constant and the string are the same datum, so a name moved in the slice takes its constant and its convar with it. That is the ammo_failover bug made impossible rather than commented about.

Round trip proved, all 22 byte for byte. The test parses the real features.sp, pulls the enum block, the FEATURE_NAME array and the MakeFeature calls, and reconstructs the convar the way MakeFeature does, which is the format string indexed by enum position, precisely the join the bug broke. Name, constant, convar, default and description compare equal as 22 named subtests. Verified here at 38 tests passing with no skips.

The proof is itself proved: TestFeatureProofCatchesASwappedName exchanges two names in the generated array and fails if the comparison still passes.

Not done here: the generated file has never been through spcomp, and adoption is filed as mvm-z83.16. Until then this round trips but is not known to compile.

The wave record is one Go declaration of 112 fields, each carrying its json name, its format verb and its SourcePawn argument. The Go field name and Go type are derived, not transcribed. It emits the FormatEx in mvmbots_stats.sp and the tagged Go struct the report unmarshals.

Round trip proved, all 112 fields matching on name, verb and argument expression, in order. Placeholders and arguments are counted against each other, so a format string with one more %d than arguments fails at the table rather than shifting every field after it, which is the failure mode that made a renamed field read as a zero.

Every json tag testbed/report/main.go reads today is a field the writer writes. TestWaveProofCatchesARenamedField renames robot_kills and fails if the comparison still passes.

Not done here: testbed/report/main.go still hand writes its own subset struct. Proved to be a subset, not replaced, because that is a change in the plugin repository. Filed with adoption in mvm-z83.16.

The checker accepts the subset and refuses everything else at file:line:col with the replacement named, not just the construct. 66 tests green: 48 refusal cases, 13 acceptance cases, and tests asserting every refusal carries both a position and a non-empty fix. Verified here.

The subset is in internal/gosubset/SUBSET.md. Sized types only, no int or uint, since a cell is 32 bits and the width should be written. No strings, slices, maps, pointers, interfaces, closures or allocation.

range and len are accepted without type information, and SUBSET.md argues why that is sound rather than lucky: the type rules leave nothing to range over but an array or an integer, because no slice, map, channel or function value can be declared or imported.

Taken from SourceGo under MIT, attribution in ATTRIBUTION.md. pass1_illegal_code is the same refusal list and all of it was kept. pass3_merge_rettypes is why several return values are accepted, the generator turning results after the first into by-reference parameters, and correspondingly why pointers are refused in author code: the only pointers in the output are the ones the generator puts there. pass9 is why range is accepted, pass10 why a discarded call result is. Rejected: pass1 permits map[string]V onto StringMap, and this subset has neither strings nor maps.

The subset was checked against the real code rather than invented. ThreatPriority and SelectMoreDangerousThreat fit exactly, with the engine reads becoming fields on a struct the caller fills, which is the never-call-back rule working. ScoreNestArea and its helpers fit once the ArrayList walks become a fixed array plus a count. Both are in testdata as acceptance tests.

The includes are parsed and Go is emitted. Nothing is transcribed, which was the whole point against forking SourceGo's 36 hand written files.

Over 204 .inc files: 1175 natives, 915 stocks, 112 methodmaps, 1531 methods, 310 properties, 253 enums, 35 typedefs, 1961 defines. The natives, methodmaps and properties counts are asserted equal to a grep of the declaration lines, so a parser that silently swallows a declaration fails the test rather than under-reporting.

Refusals are loud and counted. 70 parse refusals, all deliberate: 35 typeset, 33 operator overloads, 1 destructor, 1 function-like macro. 97 emit refusals: 70 variadic format functions, 22 defines whose body is not a constant expression, and a genuine duplicate in the source where actions.inc declares BehaviorAction.Set at both :895 and :900. Threading each file's resolved constants into the next drops define refusals from 69 to 22.

Cross-checked against what the plugin actually calls: of 1216 distinct capitalised call sites, 293 resolve to a free native or stock, 150 to a methodmap member, 758 are the plugin's own, and 15 are unaccounted. 14 of those are the plugin's own enum struct fields the definition regex misses. One is real and is filed separately. The external surface is covered.

The finding that would have been a silent wrong answer: SourcePawn passes arrays by reference, so a non-const float vec[3] emits as a pointer to array while const stays a value. Getting that backwards drops every out-parameter write with no error anywhere.

Verified here: go test -race green across the repository, golangci-lint 0 issues, make check passes end to end.

CheckFiles collects package level types and functions from every file before checking any file. CheckDir parses the directory and calls it once; CheckFile is CheckFiles over one file, so single file use is unchanged.

Measured on the actionsel split as a fixture: per file, domain.go 0 refusals, select.go 12, shipped.go 12. Twenty four false refusals. CheckDir over the same three files: 0.

The two tests that matter are the ones guarding against a rubber stamp. TestUnknownNamesAcrossFiles is table driven over a two file package where the second file reaches for a name no file declares, ten cases, all refused. TestSingleFileCannotSeeThePackage pins the single file gap in place so it stays observable rather than becoming a surprise.

One bug found on the way: an import name is file scoped in Go, and carrying imports forward would have accepted a selector the next file never imported. beginFile resets them, and TestImportsDoNotLeakBetweenFiles asserts the refusal lands in the file that did not import.

Verified here: 82 tests, go build clean, golangci-lint 0 issues.

Height relative to the surround is now what the verdict is computed from rather than a column somebody reads. SurroundHeight returns the highest surface within reach, and Footing is decided as off the mesh, then raised, then pocket, then ground.

Raised is tested before the footprint on purpose, and that is what found the fourth relocated spot. A coordinate can stand 79 over its surround and still have an area's footprint reach under it 79 below, which Coaltown DispenserSpot 2 does. The old rule missed it entirely because it only ever asked whether there was a footprint.

The reading is not borderline and there is a test saying so: the highest ground level hole reads 4, the lowest rock top reads 60, and the 18 unit line sits in a 56 unit empty band.

The three Bigrock spots the maintainer caught now classify as spot-relocated rather than as holes, so the tool agrees with the bead text that was corrected by hand.

internal/navmesh/check.go: seven rules, three severities in the project's own vocabulary. Note, degraded meaning the spot is not honoured and the bot arrives somewhere else, broken meaning the bot cannot arrive. Twelve findings over the seven maps that have a mesh.

  no-spots              broken    fires 0, mvm-tz9 regression guard
  too-few-exits         degraded  fires 0, mvm-1pq guard
  spot-off-mesh         broken    fires 1
  spot-in-hole          broken    fires 4
  spot-relocated        degraded  fires 4
  spot-beside-fall      note      fires 1
  exit-ring-beside-fall note      fires 2

The checked table pins severity, rule and spot per map, with the numbers left in the golden so float formatting cannot break the classification test. quietRules records the two rules that fire nowhere with the reason, and a rule that goes quiet without being recorded fails the test, so a check that breaks does not read as a bug that was fixed.

One rule was deliberately narrowed after reading the plugin rather than left wide. The first cut required SniperSpot, EngineerNest and TeleporterExit and flagged 21 of 27 configs. SetupSniperSpotHints switches the map's own func_tfbot_hint entities off and logs an error when there is no sniper block, so the sniper genuinely has nothing. A missing nest or exit block falls back to the nest scorer and the bot_hint_engineer_nest entities, and a hand written block is an override rather than a requirement. So the rule requires the sniper only, and 21 configs declaring no nest is a choice.

The 20 community maps have no nav file here. NeedsMesh makes that explicit and CheckConfig with no mesh still runs the two counting rules over all 27, which is not nothing: both bugs those rules exist for were counting bugs.

The premise in this bead was wrong and the correction is the result.

ActionComponent appears zero times in source/. Zero of ActionComponentFn's three signatures are used, so it never blocked anything. What the 27 files in behavior/ actually assign is BehaviorActionListeners properties, whose types are two other typesets in actions_processors.inc: ActionHandler, 7 of 29 signatures used, and ActionContextualHandler, 5 of 7. Twelve distinct signatures live across fourteen property names. All 16 OnEnd handlers return void, so the Action-returning variant is dead here.

So neither option this bead offered was right. Picking one signature is impossible with twelve live, and hand writing one declaration in a package whose whole claim is that nothing is transcribed would have been worse, and would still have left the other 34 typesets refused.

Typesets are now generated: an opaque struct carrying the function reference, which is what the SourcePawn value is and what makes the setters compile, plus one named func type per signature carrying the include's own comment. Bead mvm-z83.11 gets an exact Go signature per callback rather than a name.

Typeset refusals across the tree: 35 to 0.

internal/bindgen. One package, not many: SourcePawn's include graph has cycles between core.inc, handles.inc and functions.inc, and Go forbids import cycles, so one package is the only shape that survives. It costs nothing because a binding has no body.

Emission order is the real #include graph topologically sorted, with ties and cycles broken in path order and pinned by a test. Options gained Names alongside Constants so the claimed identifier set threads file to file; without it two includes declaring EF_BONEMERGE produce a package that does not compile.

The proof is a build, not a harness. TestGeneratedPackageBuilds writes 205 files and a go.mod to a temp dir and runs go build with no hand edits. Define refusals landed at 22, matching this bead's prediction.

Two collateral fixes the build forced. The emitted receiver is now this, because nav.inc has a method whose parameter is x and collided with the old receiver. Trailing variadics are rendered rather than refused, because Go can express them and refusing them was wrong; that alone took refusals from 177 to 107.

One generated file holds tags no include declares, and the list is one name, Function. A test caps it at twelve, because anything longer would mean a refusal upstream reappearing as an invented type.

The parity edge is zero. Unbound compares 1085 free call sites and 188 member uses against what the package declares: no unbound natives and no unbound methodmap members. Getting there needed a Code helper that blanks comments and string literals first, because the plugin passes VScript as strings and keeps commented-out prototypes beside the code, which were producing six phantom missing natives.

Limits recorded: Unbound is a name comparison and not a type check, so zero is a floor on the hand written remainder rather than proof of correctness. go build proves the package compiles and not that a binding is right; every body panics and signature fidelity rests on four golden files.
